writing.explanation:
With choices [0,1,1,3], index 0 selects 10, index 1 selects 20, index 2 retains 20, and index 3 selects 40. Each index i replaces with probability 1/(i+1); the exact replacement rule is now explicit.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Parse equally sized values and choices arrays. At zero-based index i, choices[i] is in 0..=i; replace the one-item reservoir exactly when choices[i] == i. Return the selected value, or none for empty arrays. The visible fixture is `values=[10,20,30,40]; choices=[0,1,1,3]` and its example result is `40`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Reservoir Sampling when it asks for uniform sampling from streams and files too large for memory. Here the concrete task is: Parse equally sized values and choices arrays. At zero-based index i, choices[i] is in 0..=i; replace the one-item reservoir exactly when choices[i] == i. Return the selected value, or none for empty arrays. The visible input `values=[10,20,30,40]; choices=[0,1,1,3]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Ask whether one pass is enough, whether order matters, and whether a later query will need information you already discarded. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Replace a fixed reservoir with decreasing probability while streaming unknown-length input. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A scan turns a sequence into a small piece of state. Say what the state means after the first i elements, before you describe a loop body. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n) time · O(1) reservoir state for k=1; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `40` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Use an empty slice and a one-element slice as checks. Initial values must not silently assume that at least one item exists. A borrowed slice and a for loop usually express the traversal clearly; distinguish an index you need to return from a value you merely read. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
